sentences.text: Oplosaurus is known from a single tooth that has often been linked to the genus Pelorosaurus, but there is no solid evidence supporting this connection.
A large reptilian tooth was reported by geologist Thomas Wright in 1852 from the Wealden Clay near Brixton Bay on the Isle of Wight.
French paleontologist Paul Gervais established the type species Oplosaurus armatus in 1852 based on the tooth found by Thomas Wright.
The holotype tooth of Oplosaurus is 85 mm tall in total, with a spatulate crown measuring 52 mm, a size comparable to that of Brachiosaurus.
The generic name Oplosaurus is derived from the Greek word hoplon, which means "body armour".
Recent research suggests Paul Gervais may have intended the name Oplosaurus to mean "armed lizard," interpreting the teeth as weapons of a carnivore rather than armor.
The size of the Oplosaurus tooth, comparable to that of Brachiosaurus, indicates the animal was a large sauropod, a conclusion that holds even if it is classified as a turiasaur.
Oplosaurus was likely a quadrupedal herbivore reaching a length of approximately 25 meters (82 feet).
Oplosaurus likely belongs to the broader group Macronaria.
Regardless of specific family placement, Oplosaurus likely belongs to the general group Macronaria.

Oplosaurus armatus is the only known species of the dubious extinct genus Oplosaurus, a sauropod dinosaur that lived approximately 130 million years ago during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Europe.
Oplosaurus lived between the Valanginian and Barremian stages, approximately 137.05 to 121.4 million years ago.
There is an open debate regarding the classification of Oplosaurus, with some researchers suggesting it is a turiasaur while others conclude it is a member of the Camarasauridae.

It is debated whether the name Oplosaurus originally referred to an armored dinosaur or an armed carnivore, with recent research suggesting Gervais compared the tooth to Mosasaurus rather than Hylaeosaurus.
